title: Optimizing Data Visualization Library Distribution
business: A team developing a modular data visualization library for web developers.
problem: The library contains dozens of specialized chart types, but users only need one or two. Bundling the entire library forces end-users to download massive, unused code blocks, increasing page load times.
solution: Rollup utilizes ES module static analysis to perform tree-shaking, which identifies and excludes unused functions from the final bundle, ensuring only the necessary code is shipped.
steps: Refactor the library codebase to use ES6 import and export statements for all internal modules.
Configure the Rollup build process to target multiple output formats, specifically ES modules for modern bundlers and CommonJS for legacy Node.js compatibility.
Define the entry point in the package.json file to point to the compiled CommonJS output.
Add a module field in package.json that points to the ES module version to enable tree-shaking for end-users.
Execute the Rollup build command to generate the optimized bundles.
outcome: End-users receive significantly smaller bundles because Rollup strips out the unused chart components during the build process.
limitation: Rollup's tree-shaking relies on static analysis of ES modules; dynamic imports or side-effect-heavy code can prevent the bundler from safely removing unused exports, which can be verified by inspecting the final bundle output for unexpected code remnants.

questions.question: In Optimizing Data Visualization Library Distribution, how does Rollup address the problem of shipping unused code?
options: By automatically minifying all variable names to reduce file size.
By statically analyzing ES modules to exclude unused functions from the final bundle.
By forcing users to manually select which modules to include in their project.
By converting all CommonJS modules into a single, monolithic file.
questions.explanation: The scenario describes using tree-shaking to identify and remove unused code, which is the core mechanism Rollup uses to solve the bloat problem.
questions.evidence: Rollup utilizes ES module static analysis to perform tree-shaking, which identifies and excludes unused functions from the final bundle, ensuring only the necessary code is shipped.

questions.question: In Optimizing Data Visualization Library Distribution, what is a primary limitation of the tree-shaking process?
options: It only works if the library is written in CommonJS format.
It requires the developer to manually delete unused code before building.
Dynamic imports or side-effect-heavy code can prevent the bundler from safely removing unused exports.
It increases the complexity of the final bundle by adding extra dependencies.
questions.explanation: Tree-shaking relies on static analysis; code patterns that obscure the module graph, such as dynamic imports or side effects, hinder the bundler's ability to prune the tree.
questions.evidence: Rollup's tree-shaking relies on static analysis of ES modules; dynamic imports or side-effect-heavy code can prevent the bundler from safely removing unused exports, which can be verified by inspecting the final bundle output for unexpected code remnants.
